This sector must be brought into the tax net, but not by burdening the end consumer. Therefore, let's give the dividends from the profits generated by the old projects, invested by the Nepali state for 30, 34 years, to the Nepali people in the form of dividends. And in this way, it will appear in the bill as VAT, but the amount will not increase by a single paisa, and the bill's charges will not increase. We are exercising that option, either by adjusting the price itself or by seeing if the free units can be increased from 50 to 50, 100, or 150. We are doing homework on this. Therefore, I have informed the honorable members about this repeatedly. And regarding education and health, it is not applicable to government and community schools. Now, if you are spending five thousand rupees to educate your children, and you are spending on education, then 3 percent of that is 150 rupees. With that 150 rupees, we can invest in the development of community and public schools in Dolakha, Jumla, and marginalized communities for nutrition and improvement. This is also based on the principle of progressivity. Although there was significant criticism regarding this, we have stated in our tax policy that even if you spend on private schools for children, you can get a tax deduction of 24,000 rupees or 25 percent, whichever is less. We have provided this facility. Therefore, this cannot be attacked from any angle; it has been thought through very carefully. But why was it done? Concessions were given here, taxes were imposed there, concessions were given here – what was done? To create a system, to bring it into the system, to mold it, to build an economy, to build a country, to lay the foundation for ten, twenty, thirty years from today. Therefore, we have chosen the slightly unpopular, unappealing path, whether to shy away from temporary discomfort or to face the risks head-on. But we are finding that if we explain it to the public, we will get their support, and this is being confirmed. Now, regarding reforms in tax administration, etc., the honorable members have also raised these points. I believe all the objectives raised by Honorable Prem Prasad Dahal have been reflected in the budget's revenue policy. Therefore, I expect that you will be happy if you send it back for reconsideration. However, its implementation, which is the core intent, is challenging. And today, I have two pillars of Nepal's revenue system, two institutions: the Inland Revenue Department and the Customs Department. We have set a target of collecting 1480 billion this year and 1580 billion next year. To manage both institutions in a new way, new leadership, capable, honest individuals have been appointed today, and I hope that this time we will move towards achieving our ambitious goals. Last year, the target was 1480 billion, but only about 1200 billion has been collected so far. If we reach 1300 billion by the end of the fiscal year, we will be happy. Therefore, a major reform is needed here. We need to stop leakages, adopt technology, and through digitalization, voluntary tax compliance, and most importantly, leadership with integrity and competence, this is possible, and we have moved forward with this belief. Regarding the issues raised by Honorable Khamm Khalti, I have taken note of both positive and negative aspects. From the revenue collection target to alternative plans if revenue is not collected, expenditure cuts will be necessary. It's simple. This year too, the target was 1480 billion. If it's not met, expenditures will be cut proportionally. There will be some broad sharing of that. Cuts may occur at the local level, at the provincial level, and at the federal level. However, sometimes, even if expenditure titles are not met, the revenue target, when slightly reduced, seems to come into balance in the end. Nevertheless, we want to work on the credibility of the budget. Therefore, our effort in the coming year will be with the goal of implementing it at the announced scale. I have already responded repeatedly regarding errors and so on. Regarding electricity and other matters, the tax policy is directed towards digitalization, modernization, and promoting productive industries. I thank you for recognizing that. Thank you.

Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable members, the discussion on the proposal to consider the Bill to Raise National Debt, 2083, received with a message from the House of Representatives, will now begin. I inform you that only the theoretical aspect of the bill will be discussed in this context. I request honorable members who wish to participate in the discussion to submit their names within 2 minutes. Each honorable member participating in the discussion has been allocated 3 minutes. Honorable member Prem Prasad Dahal.
Honorable Mr. Prem Prasad Dahal (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, Sir, I have studied the Bill to Regulate Raising National Debt, recently presented by the Honorable Finance Minister. Since it is short, I studied it; it is only one and a half pages, at most two pages. Through this dependent bill, the government has committed to raising 4 trillion 10 billion in debt. Now, why take debt? While discussing the theoretical aspect, we need to consider why debt is necessary, why take debt. In fact, the Honorable Finance Minister has already discussed this. It is a matter we all feel: we have not been able to make our economy self-reliant. This is true in all sectors. Agriculture, industry, tourism, services, the situation is the same in all sectors. Simultaneously, we have not been able to increase productivity. We have not been able to increase production, nor have we been able to increase productivity. Why? Because out of 60% of the working population engaged in agriculture, how much are they producing? They are producing about one-fourth. This is the economic situation. On the other hand, 40% of the citizens are engaged and producing 75%, where productivity is high. Therefore, our current phase is to focus on increasing production and productivity.
To accomplish this task, we need to increase investment in productive sectors. If we do this, economic activities will increase. The country can move towards industrialization, employment can be created, and exports can be promoted.
I want to raise a point here: what is the effectiveness of the utilization of debt? It is again related to production. It is related to employment, infrastructure, and economic growth rate. Its use is necessary in these areas.
A significant aspect of this is good governance and corruption. It is necessary to adopt a strict monitoring process to prevent irregularities in projects funded by debt. Project chiefs and civil servants there need to be held accountable. Offices like the Prime Minister's Office, Parliament, and other committees should monitor them; attention needs to be paid to such matters. Similarly, regarding debt stability, debt sustainability, we need to take debt by considering the size of public debt, its proportion to GDP, and our ability to repay debt in the future. And finally, transparency and accountability. The process of taking debt, spending it, and monitoring it must be transparent and accountable, and parliamentary roles must be present somewhere. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable member Kiran Babu Shrestha.
Honorable Mr. Kiran Babu Shrestha (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, Sir, as per the constitutional provision, the Bill to Raise National Debt, 2083, has been presented in the Parliament. Since this is a constitutional provision, the Finance Minister presents it every year, and we discuss it. Now, in the discussion, we raise some points, and the Finance Minister has a ready-made answer. It is appropriate to take debt; debt is needed for the country, for development. But where should the debt be spent? All honorable members raise questions about spending it in productive sectors, and the Finance Minister's ready-made answer is, 'We will do it in this way, we are for that.'
In the context of these questions, today I want to draw the special attention of the Finance Minister and also caution him. We need to discuss and evaluate how justified the debts we took in the past were and how well they were justified. Nepal's public debt is increasing day by day. But we raise new debt every year, yet we do not see the expected achievements in economic growth, production, employment, and capital formation accordingly. Similarly, I would like to request the Finance Minister to establish a tradition of clearly showing the return on investment from debt to the Parliament, not just the amount of debt. And there is an old saying, and not just a saying, 'Borrow and drink ghee' was a practice in the past. I also request that such a tradition and situation do not persist forever. There is a saying, one can build a house by taking debt, but if one spends that debt on daily needs without losing discretion, that debt can be lost tomorrow. I think we all need to pay attention to that, and the increasing amount of debt every year also shows our economic condition. Similarly, if medicine is given to a sick person but the disease does not get cured, one should not increase the amount of medicine. I think attention should be paid to identifying the cause of the disease and finding out what the disease is. Therefore, if a farmer takes a loan to buy seeds, that loan brings greenery to the field. But if that loan is spent on daily expenses, then when the next harvest comes, the debt cannot be repaid. Therefore, let these debts taken today not become a burden for future generations, and in the future, the country... Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable member Ram Kumari Jhakri.
Honorable Ms. Ram Kumari Jhakri (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honorable Chairperson, Sir, the narrative that is being spread to defame Nepali politics regarding public debt is that foreign debt is increasing, and a false narrative has been created. The truth is that this increase in debt is a trend in recent times. But the previous government or responsible people did not say where it was spent. Therefore, I expect the Honorable Finance Minister to tell us what the benefit of our investment is. Because in the economic survey released in February 2082, we saw that the parameters we changed, the data we altered, and the changes we saw in people's lives were due to this public debt, this mobilization of public debt, and I think it is indirect. What happened directly? The size of GDP should increase, employment should be created. There may be some geopolitical reasons for this. Therefore, taking internal or external debt to balance income and expenditure is our trend; it happens all over the world, and there is a practice of taking debt within a certain limit. But how to define its productivity? Yesterday, we talked about the implementation of fundamental rights in the constitution, and we did many other things like education and health. Indirectly, it has been done in infrastructure development, water supply, etc. Now, we need to talk about sufficient drinking water, and there are many other things to do. To fulfill our national and international commitments, debt and budget arrangements are also made for these reasons. Therefore, this narrative was started in a bad way yesterday. But this narrative needs to be done in the right way now. Because when the Honorable Finance Minister was a Member of Parliament, a shadow minister, I felt ashamed of taking this 6 trillion debt. But now, when this total debt is becoming 30 trillion, you have to say that our productivity has gone there. Therefore, its benefit is today in our lives, in the lives of our mothers, in the lives of those who died unable to give birth, in the lives of our sisters and children. We have received it in these places, and we have to say that we still have a lot to do. It's not just about changing lives; it's also about resilience. What kind of city to live in, what kind of roads to use, what kind of vehicles to drive, or how to live, what to do – the state has to invest in many aspects of life. Because we are moving towards neoliberalism, and we are talking about social justice, even if the Finance Minister says so, he has not ignored the fundamentals of a welfare state in this budget. Therefore, since we are all in this, we have to bring the budget and programs within its scope and limits, so the correct information needs to be given to the public. Why has our politics become bad? When people say this, the cement put in the cowshed of the farmer, the improved stove, the siphon put in the toilet – we have run all these with this debt. We need to pay attention to this. Thank you.
Honorable Chairperson:- Honorable member Padam Bahadur Pariyar.
Honorable Mr. Padam Bahadur Pariyar (Nepali Congress):- Honorable Chairperson, Sir, while discussing the Bill to Regulate Raising National Debt, the Honorable Finance Minister has arranged to raise approximately 410 billion in domestic debt within the budget of 2184 billion presented. If we also add the figure of external debt, it comes to about 657 billion. In this way, when the budget is presented next year, our domestic debt, our total debt, can be estimated to reach approximately 36 trillion. What can be said from all these things is that the Minister has just taken 25 billion in debt yesterday. What does this show? Are we slowly falling into a debt trap? In the current situation, we are spending one-fifth of our total budget on repaying debt. We have also heard about the increase in debt from the previous Honorable Minister. My question to the Honorable Minister is: after becoming the Finance Minister, what kind of structural, what kind of policy-level reforms are you going to make for the best utilization of this, so that our public debt can be best utilized? I would like some answer from the Finance Minister regarding that. Thank you.

(5:16 PM) The discussion on the proposal to consider the National Debt Raising Bill, 2083, is now concluded. Honorable members, I now provide time to the Honorable Finance Minister, Dr. Swarnim Wagle, to respond to the questions raised in the discussion.

Honorable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle: Honorable Chairperson, I wish to respond to the questions raised regarding the National Debt Raising Bill. This debt is something we look at in aggregate; it's a stock. It's an accumulation, a stock that has been taken and repaid, with additions, since 30, 40, 50 years ago. We always look at this in relation to the size of the economy. GDP is a flow, an annual production, annual income. Therefore, it's not usually possible to divide this stock by the flow. However, in this field, we have always discussed matters in terms of the Debt-to-GDP ratio. I have repeatedly stated that figures like 30 trillion, 32 trillion, or 50 trillion are inherently meaningless on their own. For instance, 30 trillion might be a bit high for Nepal in a particular context or situation, but for a country like Vanuatu in the Pacific Ocean, it would be extremely large, while for our southern neighbor India or northern neighbor China, it would be very small. Therefore, to determine if it's large or small, we always use GDP as a benchmark. So, let me start from the end. Honorable Padam Bahadur Pariyar mentioned that it reached 36 trillion this year. That itself wouldn't be a problem if we increased GDP in the same proportion. So, if we increase the current GDP of 66 trillion to about 74 trillion and 60 billion, paradoxically, the current ratio will decrease. Our current Debt-to-GDP ratio is 44 percent. Based on the projected size of the economy, public investment, private investment, and a 7 percent real growth, if the GDP reaches 74 trillion next year, the ratio will either remain stable or decrease. Therefore, if we proceed based on that ratio, this debt is X trillion, and it's not just that it hasn't been raised or collected today, but it's being raised every year. The claim that each Nepali has X lakhs of debt on their head is misleading, and I believe we need to explain these more advanced arguments to the public. Therefore, if we keep the Debt-to-GDP ratio within a desired limit, it's not a problem. Whether it's a problem or not is determined by various benchmarks like remittance inflow, exports, other incomes, foreign exchange earnings in dollars, and whether they can sustain it, support it, and service the debt. The International Monetary Fund, of which we are a member state, evaluates this annually through Article IV consultations. It classifies most developing countries into high, medium, and low-risk categories, and Nepal has been placed in the low-risk category so far. If we can increase the pace of development and the size of the economy by taking loans, they say 'Debts should pay for themselves.' There's an understanding that debt should automatically reduce its burden through economic growth, and that is our goal. Therefore, it's not about consuming ghee by taking loans, but if we can invest it in productive activities, as the size of GDP increases and our sustainable sources of income strengthen, we can continue to service that debt. Sovereign debt is slightly different from household debt. A country's lifespan is infinite, so a direct comparison is not possible. If we proceed responsibly, the issue that is being discussed outside Parliament today, the context of these '20-second clubs,' is happening now. Wagle said he couldn't sleep when taking loans, and now it's reported that he took loans himself. That's also a product of that '20-second' incident; it was a long context. The context was that in 2015, our Debt-to-GDP ratio was only 25 percent. In seven years, we increased it to 43 percent, which is why I couldn't sleep. An 18 percentage point increase in debt in seven to eight years was a lot, extremely large, and I spoke about it to draw attention to that. It's not that debt should not exist, or that the country should be run without taking loans, as was said in the House of Representatives. That is an irresponsible statement. People can slip up occasionally, but I haven't intentionally made irresponsible statements or arguments. The issue of health insurance loans has also become a point of political attack, as honorable members understand. You have also been victims of such attacks multiple times. I will leave that matter there. The growth of 18 percentage points in seven to eight years needs to be analyzed. I know there was an earthquake, and we took loans for earthquake reconstruction. COVID-19 came, and we took all the loans we could during that period. That's why debt increased during that period; otherwise, a Debt-to-GDP ratio of 24 percent is considered very low even for our least developed country. But I am saying that if we can stabilize it up to 43-44 percent and use the borrowed loans for productive activities, there might not be a cause for alarm. Currently, even if we borrow 6.5 trillion, half of it goes to repay old loans. There is 410 billion in domestic debt, and 247 billion of that goes to repay old loans. So, the net remaining amount is very small. In foreign debt, we are borrowing a total of 247 billion, but regarding foreign debt, the President of the Asian Development Bank visited yesterday. Their loan structure is such that we borrow if we can spend. Domestic debt can always be spent, as there is liquidity, and we can raise it from the central bank ourselves. Foreign loans are repaid, so their utilization is very low. Even though we are borrowing 247 billion in foreign debt, 72 billion goes to repay old loans. Therefore, when new loans are taken to repay old loans, the total is around 303 billion. If the economy of 66 trillion reaches 74 trillion, this additional 30 trillion that we took on March 13th, the old accumulated debt, was 30 trillion. As of March 12th, the nation carried a debt burden of approximately 2975 billion. The cumulative debt taken by previous governments, while repaying and borrowing, has increased to about 30 trillion. If we borrow this year and settle everything, it might reach about 33 trillion. But if GDP grows proportionally, we can keep the ratio stable around 44-45 percent. International suggestions and recommendations are to keep it below 47-48, 50 percent for development to gain momentum; otherwise, there might not be a cause for alarm. However, as I said, the issue that caused sleeplessness was the rapid borrowing of loans in a short period, and when investigating their utility and returns, if we reach a stage of difficulty, it becomes worrying. I drew attention to that. Primarily, the loans we take, foreign loans, are for roads, power plants, transmission lines, dry ports, and similar projects, which have purposes very different from current expenses like salaries, allowances, and benefits. And what we hope for is that they will provide such high returns in the long run that 'those debts will pay for themselves.' If we spend in sectors that enhance our capacity to repay on our own, that is the direction we should be heading. Honorable members of Parliament, as ministers, our responsibility is to ensure that loans are not taken for frivolous spending or misused. We need to look into these matters. Medium-term Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA) is conducted by international organizations, and if it remains within the desired limits, it's not a problem in itself. We are in trouble because we are landlocked and our currency is not convertible. Japan has a Debt-to-GDP ratio of 220 percent, which they can bear because most of the debt is domestic, the Japanese Yen is convertible, their innovative capacity, and their economic credibility are globally established, so they can bear it. America's is around 100 percent. We cannot compare ourselves to them, but even among developing countries, we are below the average of 50-60 percent, which is why we have progressed this way. However, the main issue is what we are doing with the borrowed money and what the returns are. Since it's primarily invested in infrastructure, the quality of infrastructure varies. Loans were taken for airports, but not all airports have become functional. However, some have become very functional, reducing travel time and costs. Large highways have made the economy efficient, and their returns have likely been many times over. Therefore, I believe we need to analyze the returns on a project-by-project, case-by-case, and sector-by-sector basis.

Mandatory liabilities are around 14 trillion. Even if the state does nothing, we will spend 14 trillion. Revenue collected so far is around 12 trillion. We cannot run without taking loans. To undertake significant development construction and to bear expenses beyond current expenditures, we need to take loans, but the core issue is for what purpose, for what return, and a thorough public analysis is necessary. We also desire that our institutions conduct this. The government, when taking loans, will only proceed after mentioning the expected return in the documents. Yesterday, we took loans for logistics, trade logistics, and also for drinking water and urbanization. These are concessional loans. We have to repay them in dollars at 1-1.4 percent interest, with maturities of 30-32 years and grace periods of 7-8 years. These are very concessional loans that we have been taking, mainly from the World Bank and ADB. However, even these concessional loans are gradually shrinking. That's the concern. In the next 3-5 years, we will not get loans at this rate. The terms of interest rates or loans will become stricter, the repayment periods will shorten, and we will have to advance our development goals under extreme pressure. Therefore, we need to assess and prepare for a situation where the search for sources is becoming very complex. Thank you.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: The Minister for Physical Infrastructure Development responded to questions regarding road conditions, accidents, bridge construction, and landslide mitigation. He detailed budget allocations for road widening, bridge construction, and landslide control, emphasizing road safety measures like underpasses and overpasses. The minister also addressed issues of contractor negligence, proposed amendments to the Procurement Act, and discussed the displacement of Tuins, promising suspension bridge construction. He outlined plans for upgrading existing tourist roads and addressing challenges in the Kaligandaki Corridor due to climate change. The minister also spoke about digitalizing office processes to improve efficiency and combat corruption, and highlighted the prioritization of north-south connectivity and the 3-year plan approach over annual programs. He assured that waste management is being addressed through budget allocation and policy changes. Finally, he emphasized the significant budget allocation and focus on road development in the Sudurpashchim and Karnali provinces.

sections.name: Main Business
sections.summary_en: Honorable Member Ram Kumari Jhankri initiated the discussion on the Finance Bill, 2083, highlighting its role in policy enhancement and revenue collection. She raised ethical and public questions regarding tax rate changes and the minister's accountability, referencing past resignations of finance ministers. Honorable Member Prem Prasad Dahal focused on the bill's objectives, including economic growth, job creation, and social justice, questioning its focus on tax rates and administration. Honorable Member Khamma Bahadur Khati discussed the bill's legal basis for revenue policy, noting both positive aspects like modernization and negative aspects like investor uncertainty and lack of prioritization for SMEs. He also raised specific questions about revenue targets, inter-governmental coordination, and tax implications for essential services.
